rv.q: The result is both surprisingly funny and shockingly frank.
Menzies and D'Arcy, the entrancingly stubborn elder daughter, deliver a climax that sent a series of collective gasps of shock through the audience on the night I went.
But all these quibbles can't take away from the vivid family dynamic that Zeldin and his cast create here.

The urn of ashes is constantly being decanted into a Ziploc bag in a tug-of-war that’s partly a farce, with Jerry Killick providing laughs as the sleazebag family friend. The shock revelation I can’t spoil. But while it’s compelling to watch, it’s got a feel of wilful obscurity and it lacks the stark, epic quality of the classic it vaguely recycles.
The malnourished torpor appealed to the depressive masochist in me, but needn't detain better-adjusted theatre-goers.
The Other Place feels slight and needs more time to establish the characters and make their desire to be free of their grief more tangible.
This is a thrilling production both written and directed by Zeldin, with perfectly layered, intersecting character arcs and a quietly menacing tone throughout.

Here, in a modern kitchen set with patio doors (much discussed in a mumbly sort of way)  we have a family gathering headed by the excellent Tobias Menzies as Uncle Chris. This fine actor will be required in turn to be sensible , a bit controlling and normal, then shouty, and borderline deranged by the end.
